title: Accessing Industry Research, Data, and Competitive Intelligence

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Identify and describe the primary Nigerian insurance industry data sources (including the NIA Annual Statistics Report, NAICOM Annual Report, NBS surveys, EFInA Access to Finance data, PenCom Annual Report, and NHIA sector data) and explain what each source provides, its publication frequency, and its appropriate use in strategy and research.

Identify and describe the principal international insurance research and benchmark sources (including the IAIS GIMAR, Swiss Re Sigma, Munich Re publications, World Bank financial sector data, IMF Financial Stability Reports, and AXCO Insurance Information) and explain how each source is used in competitive benchmarking and strategic planning for Nigerian life insurers.

Describe the market intelligence tools available for competitor analysis in the Nigerian insurance market, including NAICOM and CAC financial returns, NIA market share tables, Bloomberg and Refinitiv data, and the systematic use of competitor public disclosures.

Explain the role of academic and professional journals in the research function of a Nigerian life insurer, identifying the most relevant publications for the industry and describing how academic research is translated into practical management insight.

Explain how Freedom of Information (FOI) requests and active regulatory engagement can be used as research and intelligence tools by Nigerian insurance practitioners, consistent with the Freedom of Information Act 2011 and NAICOM engagement protocols.

Design the structure and operating model of a competitive intelligence function within a Nigerian life insurance company, including the team structure, the research calendar, the standard report templates, and the stakeholder distribution mechanism.

Describe the data sources and analytical frameworks used for insurance market sizing in Nigeria, and demonstrate how market sizing analysis informs product development, geographic expansion, and distribution investment decisions.

Explain the use of primary research methods (including consumer surveys, focus groups, mystery shopping, and digital behavioural analytics) in generating consumer insight for a Nigerian life insurer’s strategy and product development.

Describe the governance mechanisms required to translate research output into management decisions, including the research-to-strategy review process, decision-ready report formats, and the accountability framework for acting on research findings.

Evaluate the quality and reliability of different research sources, applying critical assessment criteria including recency, methodological rigour, data source transparency, and applicability to the Nigerian insurance market context.

blocks.text: 36.1 Introduction: Intelligence as a Strategic Asset

blocks.h: A Nigerian life insurer that makes strategic decisions without systematic access to industry data, competitor intelligence, and consumer research is navigating by intuition in a market that is changing faster than intuition can track. The insurer whose strategy team has not read the most recent EFInA Access to Finance survey does not know the current state of insurance penetration in its target market. The insurer whose pricing team is not monitoring NAICOM’s published market returns cannot benchmark its expense ratio or loss ratio against the market. The insurer whose product team is not reading Swiss Re Sigma and Munich Re’s Africa reports is missing the global context for the trends reshaping its market.

Research and intelligence are not luxuries for large insurers with dedicated teams. They are minimum competency requirements for any insurer that wants to make decisions that are better than random, decisions grounded in evidence rather than assumption. This chapter maps the complete research and intelligence landscape available to a Nigerian life insurer: the Nigerian primary sources, the international benchmarks, the competitor intelligence tools, the academic and professional journals, and the less-obvious channels (FOI requests, regulatory engagement, primary consumer research) that sophisticated research functions use to stay ahead of their market.

The chapter also addresses the organisational infrastructure required to turn raw research access into genuine strategic intelligence: the competitive intelligence function’s design, the research calendar, the report formats, and the governance mechanisms that ensure research findings change management decisions rather than merely filing in a shared drive.

blocks.text: 36.2 Primary Nigerian Insurance Industry Data Sources

blocks.h: The research function must systematically access and monitor the Nigerian data sources that provide market-level information about the insurance industry’s size, composition, performance, and development. These sources are the foundation of any market sizing, competitive benchmarking, or strategic planning exercise.

blocks.title: NIA Annual Industry Statistics Report: Key Information

blocks.h: PUBLISHER: Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA). FREQUENCY: Annual. ACCESS: nigerianinsurers.org / available to member insurers on request.

The NIA Annual Industry Statistics Report is the most comprehensive market-level dataset on the Nigerian insurance industry. It consolidates financial returns submitted by all licensed insurers and presents aggregated data on: gross written premium by class of business (life, non-life, composite) and by insurer; net written premium; claims paid; underwriting results; investment income; total assets; and number of policies in force. The report also includes data on insurance penetration (premium as a percentage of GDP), premium density (premium per capita), and comparison with prior years.

STRATEGIC USE: Market share analysis (by premium, by class); identification of fastest-growing and declining segments; benchmarking the insurer’s own GWP growth against market growth; monitoring claims ratio and expense ratio trends across the market. The NIA report is the single most important source of factual data about the Nigerian insurance market’s current state and trajectory.

LIMITATIONS: Published approximately 12–18 months after the reference year; does not break down individual insurer data (only market-level aggregates and ranges); does not capture informal insurance or unregulated schemes.

NAICOM publishes an Annual Report covering the regulatory activities of the commission, the industry’s performance data, market conduct findings, and supervisory actions taken during the year. Unlike the NIA’s industry statistics (which are member-produced), NAICOM’s data represents the regulatory view of the market: the data it has independently verified through statutory returns and market inspections.

NAICOM’s statutory return requirements also generate a body of individual insurer data (annual financial statements, solvency margin certificates, actuarial reports) that is filed with NAICOM and may be partially accessible through regulatory disclosure requests. NAICOM periodically publishes lists of insurers’ premium income, claims ratios, and solvency positions. The research function should systematically track these disclosures as a source of competitor financial data.

Access: naicom.gov.ng. Annual Report publication timeline: typically 12 months after the reference year. Market updates: NAICOM periodically issues press releases and market conduct reports on a more frequent basis.

blocks.text: 36.2.3 National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) Consumer and Household Surveys

blocks.h: The National Bureau of Statistics conducts a range of nationally representative surveys providing data on household income, expenditure, employment, poverty, and demographic composition. The NBS surveys most relevant to insurance research are:

items.h: National Living Standards Survey (NLSS): A comprehensive household survey providing data on income distribution, household expenditure patterns, and poverty levels by state and region. The NLSS data enables insurance market sizing by income segment and affordability analysis for product pricing.

Labour Force Survey: Data on employment status, occupation, and industry of employment. Enables estimation of the formal sector workforce (the primary target market for employer-sponsored group life and health) and the self-employed population (the target for personal pension and individual life products).

Nigeria Gross Domestic Product (GDP) Reports: Quarterly GDP data by sector; used for calculating insurance penetration ratios (insurance premium as a percentage of GDP) and for economic scenario planning.

blocks.h: Access: nigerianstat.gov.ng. Publication frequency: varies by survey type; NLSS is conducted every 3–5 years; Labour Force Survey is semi-annual; GDP data is quarterly.

blocks.text: 36.2.4 EFInA Access to Financial Services in Nigeria Survey

blocks.h: The EFInA (Enhancing Financial Innovation and Access) Access to Financial Services in Nigeria (A2F) survey is the most important demand-side data source for Nigerian insurance market research. Conducted every two years, the A2F survey interviews a nationally representative sample of approximately 20,000+ Nigerian adults, collecting data on: their use of and access to financial services (banking, insurance, credit, savings, and payments); their financial literacy levels; their attitudes toward insurance and other financial products; the barriers that prevent them from using formal financial services; and their income, employment, and demographic characteristics.
For the insurance research function, the EFInA A2F survey provides data that is available nowhere else:

items.h: Insurance penetration by demographic group: What proportion of Nigerian adults use formal insurance? How does this vary by age, gender, income, education, urban/rural location, and state of residence?

Informal insurance usage: What proportion of Nigerians use informal insurance mechanisms (Ajo, Esusu, cooperative, family support)? What needs are these mechanisms serving that formal insurance is not?

Barriers to formal insurance: Why do Nigerians who do not have insurance not have it? Affordability? Awareness? Trust? Product design? The barrier data directly informs product development, distribution strategy, and consumer education priorities.

blocks.h: Access: efina.org.ng. Frequency: biennial (every 2 years). The most recent survey data should be the foundation of any strategic planning document that claims to understand the Nigerian insurance consumer.

blocks.text: 36.2.5 PenCom Annual Report and Statistical Bulletin

blocks.h: The National Pension Commission (PenCom) publishes an Annual Report and a Quarterly Statistical Bulletin providing data on the Nigerian pension system: total pension assets under management; the number of active RSA contributors; contribution flows; investment portfolio allocation; and the number and value of Retirement Life Annuity placements. For any insurer active in the annuity market, this is essential operational intelligence.

The PenCom data enables an insurer to estimate: the total RLA market size in any year; the market share of each approved RLA provider (partially inferred from total placement data); the distribution of RSA balances (to estimate the average RLA premium per transaction); and the growth trajectory of the pension asset base as more Nigerians complete their CPS accumulation phase and approach retirement.
Access: pencom.gov.ng. The Annual Report is published approximately 6–12 months after the reference year.

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) publishes data on the licensed HMO sector: the number of licensed HMOs, their total enrollee base, gross premium income, claims paid, and geographic distribution. For insurers with health insurance operations or considering market entry into health, the NHIA data provides the regulatory-verified picture of a sector that has historically been poorly documented.

The NHIA data should be supplemented with direct inquiry to the NHIA’s licensing and supervision department, which can provide more granular data on specific scheme types, geographic distribution of HMO capacity, and compliance status of licensed HMOs (useful for competitive intelligence on potential distribution partners or targets).
Access: nhia.gov.ng. Data availability is less systematic than NAICOM’s; direct regulatory engagement is often required to obtain the most current data.

The Nigerian insurance market does not exist in isolation. It is shaped by the same global forces of technology disruption, demographic change, regulatory evolution, and macroeconomic pressure that shape insurance markets worldwide. International research and benchmark sources provide the global context that helps Nigerian practitioners understand where their market sits in the world, what trends are approaching from more developed markets, and what best practices from comparable emerging markets are most applicable.

The International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) publishes the Global Insurance Market Report (GIMAR) annually, providing a comprehensive assessment of the global insurance sector’s financial condition, systemic risks, and supervisory developments. For Nigerian insurance professionals, the GIMAR serves two specific purposes: it provides global benchmarks for insurance penetration, density, and solvency ratios against which Nigerian performance can be compared; and it identifies emerging global supervisory trends (such as the development of Risk-Based Capital frameworks and IFRS 17 implementation challenges) that foreshadow the direction of Nigerian regulatory reform.

The IAIS also publishes the Insurance Core Principles (ICPs) and their assessment methodology; the global standards against which NAICOM’s supervisory framework is evaluated in FSAP (Financial Sector Assessment Programme) assessments conducted by the IMF and World Bank. Understanding the ICPs helps insurance professionals anticipate the direction of Nigerian regulatory evolution.
Access: iaisweb.org. The GIMAR is published annually; Insurance Core Principles documentation is available permanently on the IAIS website.

Swiss Re Institute’s Sigma publication series is the global insurance industry’s most authoritative research reference. Published several times per year, individual Sigma reports address specific topics of strategic relevance: the state of the global insurance market (with country-level data on premium volumes, penetration, and density); emerging risks (climate change, pandemic, cyber); insurance in specific regional markets (Africa is covered periodically); distribution innovation; and the economics of insurance in developing markets.

For the Nigerian research function, Sigma’s African insurance market reports, and its annual ‘World Insurance’ report providing country-level data, provide the global benchmarking context for Nigerian market positioning. When a Nigerian insurer’s strategy document states that ‘Nigeria’s insurance penetration is below the African average’, it is typically relying on Swiss Re Sigma data for that benchmark.
Access: swissre.com/institute. Sigma reports are freely downloadable. The annual ‘World Insurance’ Sigma is the essential Nigerian benchmarking reference.

Munich Re’s research team produces a wide range of publications relevant to the Nigerian market: the annual ‘Natural Catastrophe Statistics’ (essential for Nigerian disaster risk and parametric insurance market analysis); the ‘Insurance Market Outlook’ covering emerging markets; specific publications on African insurance market development, agricultural insurance, health insurance in low-income markets, and Insurtech.

Munich Re’s publications are distinguished by their technical depth and their integration of actuarial, economic, and strategic perspectives. They are particularly valuable for underwriting and product development teams seeking the latest data on specific risk categories: flood risk in Nigeria, climate change’s impact on agricultural insurance losses, mortality improvement trends in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Access: munichre.com/publications. Most research publications are freely downloadable; some require registration.

blocks.text: 36.3.4 World Bank Financial Sector Data and Reports

blocks.h: The World Bank’s Global Financial Development database provides cross-country data on financial sector development including insurance penetration, insurance density, and insurance sector assets as a percentage of GDP. The World Bank’s Finance, Competitiveness and Innovation Global Practice also produces country-specific Financial Sector Assessments, Financial Inclusion Insights reports, and technical assistance outputs on insurance market development that are directly relevant to the Nigerian context.

The World Bank’s Access to Finance surveys in emerging markets (conducted in partnership with organisations like the IFC and EFInA) provide demand-side data on financial inclusion that complements the NBS and EFInA data specific to Nigeria. The World Bank’s Doing Business and Enterprise Surveys also contain information on insurance usage by Nigerian businesses that supplements the consumer-focused EFInA data.
Access: worldbank.org/en/research. The Global Financial Development database is freely searchable online; country-specific reports are downloadable.

blocks.text: 36.3.5 IMF Financial Stability Reports and Article IV Consultations

blocks.h: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) conducts annual Article IV Consultations with Nigeria, producing a publicly available Staff Report that assesses the Nigerian economy’s financial condition, risks, and reform priorities. These reports contain macroeconomic data, financial sector stability assessments, and IMF staff recommendations that provide an authoritative external perspective on the economic environment within which Nigerian life insurers operate.

The IMF also conducts periodic Financial Sector Assessment Programme (FSAP) assessments of Nigeria’s financial sector, including its insurance sector. FSAP reports provide a detailed evaluation of NAICOM’s supervisory effectiveness against the IAIS ICPs, identifying strengths and weaknesses in the regulatory framework. For strategy and risk management teams, FSAP findings are a leading indicator of areas where NAICOM will face international pressure to strengthen its supervisory framework, and therefore where regulatory change is likely to materialise.
Access: imf.org/en/publications. Article IV Staff Reports are publicly available; FSAP reports are published with the Nigerian government’s consent.

AXCO (now part of Acumen Intelligence) provides country-specific insurance market reports covering the regulatory framework, product lines, distribution channels, market structure, and key statistics for over 150 countries including Nigeria. AXCO’s Nigeria Non-Life and Life reports are a comprehensive, regularly updated reference for the Nigerian insurance market’s regulatory and commercial environment.

AXCO reports are particularly valuable for: comparative analysis of Nigerian insurance regulation against other African markets; understanding the specific regulatory requirements for market entry or product development; and providing international reinsurers and investors with a standardised overview of the Nigerian market’s structure and performance. The AXCO Nigeria reports are a required reference for any international reinsurer or investor conducting due diligence on the Nigerian market.

Access: axco.com. AXCO reports are subscription-based; individual country reports are available for purchase. Many international reinsurers, investment banks, and law firms subscribe to AXCO on behalf of their Nigerian market work.
Beyond the six core sources described above, the Nigerian insurance research function should systematically monitor:

items.h: A2ii (Access to Insurance Initiative): The most specialised source of information on inclusive insurance regulation and microinsurance in emerging markets. a2ii.org provides regulatory guidance notes, market analysis, and technical publications on microinsurance, agricultural insurance, and digital insurance in developing markets.

IFC (International Finance Corporation): The World Bank Group’s private sector arm; publishes research and case studies on insurance market development, private sector investment in African insurance, and Insurtech in emerging markets.

GSMA Intelligence: The mobile industry’s global research body; annual ‘State of the Industry Report on Mobile Money’ provides the most authoritative data on mobile money penetration and usage in Nigeria and Africa, critical for digital insurance strategy.

McKinsey Global Insurance Report: Annual publication covering global insurance industry trends, digital transformation, competitive dynamics, and strategic priorities. The Africa Insurance Outlook (periodically produced) provides the continent-specific strategic context.

Oliver Wyman, Deloitte, PwC insurance reports: The major strategy consultancies produce periodic insurance sector reports covering emerging markets. Deloitte’s ‘Insurance Industry Outlook’ and PwC’s ‘Insurance 2030’ research are particularly relevant for long-horizon strategic planning.

blocks.text: 36.4 Market Intelligence Tools for Competitor Analysis

blocks.h: Every licensed Nigerian insurer is required to file annual financial statements and statutory returns with NAICOM. While NAICOM does not publish individual insurer returns in the same format as the UK’s Companies House or the US SEC’s EDGAR, the information is partially accessible through several channels:

items.h: NAICOM publications: NAICOM periodically publishes market data tables showing premium income, claims ratios, and solvency margins by insurer or by size ranking. The research function should capture and archive every NAICOM publication that contains individual insurer data.

CAC (Corporate Affairs Commission) filings: All Nigerian companies, including insurers, are required to file annual audited financial statements with the CAC. These filings are technically publicly accessible through the CAC’s public register (cac.gov.ng). In practice, the CAC’s digital accessibility is improving, and the research function should systematically download and archive the audited accounts of key competitors each year.

Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX) disclosures: Listed insurance groups must file half-year and annual financial statements with the NGX in accordance with the SEC’s disclosure rules. These disclosures are accessible on the NGX website and are typically more timely and complete than CAC filings. Listed insurers’ investor presentations and earnings call transcripts (where available) provide additional qualitative intelligence on competitive strategy.

blocks.h: The NIA publishes periodic market share tables showing each member insurer’s gross written premium by class of business, expressed as a percentage of total market GWP. These tables are the most direct source of competitive market share data available in the Nigerian insurance market. They enable the research function to:

items.h: Monitor the insurer’s own market share trend over time (is the insurer growing faster than the market, at the same pace, or losing share?).
Identify competitors that are growing rapidly (potential threats or targets for analysis) and those that are declining (potential acquisition candidates or early indicators of financial stress).
Identify which classes of business are growing at market level and whether the insurer has appropriate representation in those growth areas.

blocks.h: The NIA market share data should be supplemented with NAICOM’s periodic disclosures to build the most complete competitive picture.

blocks.text: 36.4.3 Bloomberg and Refinitiv for Investment Benchmarking

blocks.h: Bloomberg Terminal and Refinitiv Eikon are the standard professional platforms for financial markets data, including Nigerian fixed-income (FGN bond yields, T-bill rates, corporate bond spreads), equity market data (NGX indices, individual stock prices for listed insurers), foreign exchange rates (USD/NGN, EUR/NGN), and macroeconomic data (inflation, interest rates, GDP).

For the Nigerian life insurer’s investment team, Bloomberg and Refinitiv provide: real-time and historical yield data for FGN bond portfolio management and ALM; benchmark yield curve data for actuarial discount rate setting; equity market data for unit-linked fund performance monitoring; and inflation and interest rate forecasts for economic scenario planning.

For the competitive intelligence function, these platforms provide access to research produced by investment banks covering Nigerian financial sector companies, including insurance groups. Investment bank research on listed Nigerian insurers (equity research, initiations of coverage, earnings estimates) provides a professional outside view of the insurer’s and its competitors’ performance and strategy.

Access: Bloomberg and Refinitiv are premium subscription platforms; the investment team typically has access through their fixed-income trading infrastructure. The research function should have dedicated access for competitive and market intelligence purposes.
Beyond publicly available data, the research function should systematically gather intelligence through direct market observation:

items.h: Competitor product monitoring: Systematically collecting and reviewing competitor product brochures, benefit illustrations, premium schedules, and terms and conditions. The research function should maintain a competitor product library, updated quarterly. A mystery shopping programme (contacting competitors’ distribution channels as a prospective customer) is a legitimate and valuable intelligence tool for understanding the competitor’s sales process, pricing, and product positioning.

Digital footprint monitoring: Tracking competitors’ websites, social media presence, app store ratings, and digital marketing campaigns provides real-time intelligence on their distribution investment, product launches, and brand positioning. Google Alerts for competitor brand names, NAICOM announcements, and industry keywords provides a basic automated monitoring capability that is available at zero cost.

Distribution channel intelligence: The insurer’s own agents, bancassurance relationship managers, and brokers regularly encounter competitors in the market. Structured mechanisms for collecting and sharing field intelligence (what products competitors are promoting, what pricing they are offering, what terms they are offering to bancassurance partners) are a valuable and often under-utilised intelligence channel.

Industry events and conferences: The NAICOM annual summit, NIA conferences, CIIN annual conference, and African Insurance Organisation meetings are intelligence-gathering opportunities: competitor presentations, product announcements, regulatory discussions, and senior management networking provide qualitative intelligence that data analysis cannot.

blocks.h: Academic and professional journals are often the last information source that busy insurance practitioners reach for, and frequently the most overlooked source of genuine intellectual value. The research function’s job is to bridge this gap: to read the journals, extract the findings that are relevant to the insurer’s strategic and product challenges, and translate them into decision-ready management insights.

blocks.text: 36.5.1 The Geneva Papers on Risk and Insurance

blocks.h: Published quarterly by the Geneva Association, the Geneva Papers is one of the most prestigious applied academic journals in the global insurance field. It publishes peer-reviewed research on insurance economics, financial stability, longevity risk, climate risk, digital insurance, health insurance policy, and the social role of insurance. The Geneva Papers bridges the gap between academic rigour and practical relevance: its contributors include both university academics and senior insurance practitioners.

For the Nigerian research function, the Geneva Papers is most valuable for: long-horizon strategic issues (longevity risk management, climate change and insurance, the economics of health insurance financing in low-income markets); regulatory benchmarking (articles comparing insurance supervisory frameworks across emerging markets); and distribution innovation (research on mobile and digital insurance in Africa and comparable markets).

Access: springer.com/journal/10713. Subscription-based; many Nigerian universities and research libraries have institutional access. Individual article access is available through JSTOR or author pre-print repositories.

Published by the American Risk and Insurance Association (ARIA), the Journal of Risk and Insurance (JRI) is the leading academic journal in insurance economics and actuarial science. It publishes research on insurance market behaviour, pricing, underwriting, reinsurance, regulation, and the economics of risk management. While primarily North American in focus, the JRI’s methodological frameworks and theoretical insights are globally applicable.

The most practically relevant JRI topics for Nigerian insurance practitioners: adverse selection and moral hazard in health and life insurance; the economics of insurance market regulation; lapse behaviour and its determinants; insurance and economic development; and the impact of financial innovation on insurance markets. These foundational research questions have direct relevance to the Nigerian market’s structural challenges.
Access: onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/15396975. Subscription-based; author pre-prints are often freely available.
The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria publishes several practitioner-oriented publications that are directly relevant to the Nigerian insurance market:

items.h: The Nigerian Journal of Insurance: A peer-reviewed journal publishing research on Nigerian insurance market development, regulatory issues, product innovation, and professional practice. Contributes CIIN CPD credit hours when articles are read and documented.

CIIN Newsletter and Technical Updates: Regular publications covering regulatory developments, CIIN examination news, professional development opportunities, and industry commentary. Essential reading for all CIIN members and examination candidates.

CIIN Conference Proceedings: Published following the CIIN Annual Conference; contain papers, presentations, and panel discussions from leading Nigerian insurance practitioners. A valuable source of current practitioner thinking on market issues.

blocks.h: Access: ciin.org.ng. Members have access to CIIN publications as part of their membership benefits.
The research function should also monitor:

items.h: Journal of Financial Regulation: Covers insurance regulation, financial stability, and prudential supervision from a law and economics perspective; relevant for regulatory intelligence and NIIRA 2025 interpretation.

British Actuarial Journal and Annals of Actuarial Science: The IFoA’s peer-reviewed publications covering actuarial science, longevity, reserving, and ERM; directly applicable to Nigerian actuarial practice.
African Development Review: African Development Bank’s research journal; covers financial inclusion, economic development, and insurance market development in African contexts.
Insurance Age (UK), Middle East Insurance Review, Insurance Asia: Trade press publications covering comparable markets; useful for distribution innovation and product development intelligence.

blocks.text: 36.6 Freedom of Information Requests and Regulatory Engagement

blocks.h: The Freedom of Information Act 2011 (FOIA) gives any Nigerian citizen or organisation the right to request and receive public records and information held by any public institution, including NAICOM, the NBS, EFInA (which receives public funding), and other government bodies relevant to the insurance market. FOIA is a legitimate and under-utilised research tool for accessing specific data that is not routinely published.

The FOIA process requires a written request specifying the information sought. The public institution must respond within 7 days (either providing the information, requesting a further period of up to 21 days, or declining with reasons). Grounds for declining a FOIA request include national security, personal privacy, and commercial confidentiality, but routine market data, aggregated financial statistics, and policy documents are generally accessible.

blocks.title: FOI Request Examples for Insurance Research

blocks.h: The following are examples of legitimate FOI requests that a Nigerian insurer’s research function might submit:

items.h: To NAICOM: ‘Please provide the aggregate gross written premium, net written premium, claims paid, and solvency margin data for all licensed life insurance companies for the financial year 2023, by company size quartile.’

To NAICOM: ‘Please provide the number of formal regulatory complaints received from policyholders in the life insurance sector for 2023–2024, categorised by nature of complaint (claims refusal, mis-selling, premium disputes).’
To NHIA: ‘Please provide the total number of enrolled lives across all licensed HMOs in Nigeria as at 31 December 2024, categorised by state.’

To NBS: ‘Please provide the methodology note and sampling frame documentation for the 2023 National Living Standards Survey, to enable appropriate use of the survey data in insurance market research.’

blocks.h: FOI requests should be specific, targeted, and grounded in the requesting party’s genuine research need. Speculative or very broad FOI requests are more likely to be resisted or to generate incomplete responses.

blocks.text: 36.6.2 Regulatory Engagement as a Research Tool

blocks.h: Active engagement with NAICOM, PenCom, NHIA, and other relevant regulators is one of the most valuable and most under-utilised research and intelligence channels available to the insurer’s research function. Regulators are not merely compliance administrators; they are the institutions most deeply informed about the state of the market, emerging risks, regulatory intent, and market conduct issues.
Constructive regulatory engagement provides intelligence that no published data source can match:

items.h: Advance signal of regulatory change: NAICOM’s consultation processes (industry forums, working groups, draft guideline consultations) provide advance warning of regulatory changes that may affect product design, distribution, capital requirements, or governance. An insurer that participates actively in consultations hears the regulator’s concerns and intentions six to twelve months before a formal guideline is issued.

Market conduct intelligence: NAICOM’s Consumer Protection Bureau’s public reports and its presentations at industry forums reveal the market conduct issues the regulator is most concerned about; the complaint types that are generating the most enforcement attention. This is advance intelligence for the insurer’s own market conduct risk management.

Regulatory clarification: Direct written inquiry to NAICOM on specific regulatory interpretation questions (the meaning of a NIIRA 2025 provision, the admissibility of a specific investment instrument, the applicability of a product approval requirement to a new digital distribution model) generates authoritative written guidance that is more reliable than any secondary interpretation.

blocks.text: 36.7 Insurance Market Sizing: Frameworks and Applications

blocks.h: Insurance market sizing (the estimation of the total potential premium income available in a defined market segment) is the foundational quantitative input to any strategic decision about product development, geographic expansion, or distribution investment. An insurer that cannot estimate the size of the market it is entering cannot evaluate whether the entry is commercially justified, cannot set realistic market share targets, and cannot communicate a credible investment case to its Board.
Top-down market sizing starts from large population or economic aggregates and progressively narrows to the addressable market:

items.h: Total population: Nigeria’s 220+ million people. This is the maximum theoretical market.
Target demographic segment: Adults aged 25–60 in the formal sector (approximately 35–40 million). This is the primary target market for individual life products.

Reachable segment: Adults in the target demographic within the insurer’s distribution reach (geographic coverage, agent network, bancassurance partner footprint). This is the served addressable market.

Conversion rate adjustment: Apply an estimated purchase conversion rate based on EFInA demand data (e.g., what proportion of the target demographic are actively considering insurance?). This gives the realistically acquirable market in a defined period.
Average premium: Multiply the acquirable market by the expected average annual premium per policy to arrive at the total premium income potential of the segment.

blocks.h: Bottom-up market sizing builds the estimate from granular data about specific employers, geographic markets, or product segments:

items.h: Group life market: NBS employment data provides the number of formal sector employees by industry and state. Pension Reform Act 2014 compliance rates from PenCom data indicate what proportion of formal sector employers are meeting their mandatory obligations. The average premium per employee (3× salary × market rate) applied to the total formal sector employment base gives the total group life market potential.

Annuity market: PenCom data on retiring RSA holders per year multiplied by the average RSA balance at retirement gives the total annual RLA market premium. This can be projected 5–10 years forward as the CPS cohort matures.

Microinsurance market: EFInA data on the unbanked and under-insured population, combined with NBS income distribution data and willingness-to-pay estimates from primary consumer research, gives a segmented estimate of the micro-premium market.

blocks.h: A well-designed competitive intelligence (CI) function in a Nigerian life insurer is a small, high-impact team embedded within the Strategy and Research department. Its mandate is specific: to monitor the external competitive, regulatory, and market environment and to translate that monitoring into actionable management intelligence. It does not conduct primary consumer research (that is a separate function); it does not manage the insurer’s own data analytics (that is the analytics function); it is specifically focused on the external environment.

rows: Designs and owns the CI agenda; manages key source subscriptions; presents intelligence findings to ExCo and Board; builds and maintains relationships with external analysts and regulatory contacts.
5–10 years insurance industry experience; strong analytical and communication skills; familiarity with financial data analysis.
Monitors and analyses NIA, NAICOM, and NGX data; maintains the competitor financial database; produces the quarterly market share and performance tracking report.
2–5 years in insurance or financial services research; proficiency in Excel, financial modelling, and data visualisation.
Monitors competitor product launches, pricing, and digital strategies; manages the competitor product library; conducts digital footprint monitoring and mystery shopping coordination.
1–3 years in insurance product management or marketing; digital literacy; attention to detail.
Research Librarian / Information Manager (part-time or shared)
Manages journal subscriptions, document library, and research archive; coordinates FOI requests; distributes external publications to relevant stakeholders.
Library science or information management background; organised and systematic.

blocks.h: A structured research calendar ensures systematic coverage of all data sources throughout the year, rather than ad hoc access driven by immediate need. The research calendar assigns specific monitoring activities to each month, ensuring that all major data releases are captured, analysed, and distributed to relevant stakeholders within a defined timeframe.

blocks.title: Illustrative Annual Research Calendar: Key Activities

blocks.h: JANUARY: Swiss Re Sigma ‘World Insurance’ annual report review (published December–January); annual competitor financial review (prior-year CAC/NGX filings); annual market share analysis from NIA statistics.

Q1 (MARCH): IMF Article IV Nigeria Staff Report review (published Q1 each year); NAICOM Annual Report review (prior year); quarterly competitor digital footprint review; quarterly market share tracking report to ExCo.

Q2 (JUNE): EFInA A2F Survey review (published periodically, biennial; schedule review to align with release); PenCom Q1 Statistical Bulletin; Geneva Papers and JRI quarterly journal scan; mid-year competitive intelligence update to strategy team.

Q3 (SEPTEMBER): Munich Re Natural Catastrophe Statistics mid-year update; NBS Labour Force Survey H1 data; NHIA sector data request (or direct regulatory inquiry); quarterly competitor digital footprint review; quarterly competitor product library update; CIIN Annual Conference intelligence debrief.

Q4 (DECEMBER): Annual strategic planning intelligence pack (synthesising all year’s research into a comprehensive market landscape briefing for the Board and ExCo); IAIS GIMAR annual review; AXCO Nigeria report update review; annual research function review and calendar planning for next year.

CONTINUOUS (MONTHLY): Google Alerts monitoring for competitor news, NAICOM press releases, and industry keywords; NAICOM website for new circulars and guidelines; NIA for new publications; mystery shopping quarterly (not monthly).

The CI function’s output should follow defined report templates that make findings consistently accessible to busy management readers. Research outputs that do not have a consistent, familiar format require readers to navigate new structures each time, reducing uptake and impact.

rows: Cover: macro and regulatory environment update; premium market data (NIA / NAICOM latest); top three competitor movements (product launches, financial results, distribution changes); EFInA or NBS data update (when released); management implications (two to three clear ‘so what?’ points). Distributed to ExCo, strategy team, product heads, and distribution heads.

Template maintained for each top-five competitor: latest GWP, market share, premium growth rate, loss ratio, expense ratio, solvency ratio, key strategic initiatives, leadership changes. Updated annually from CAC/NGX/NAICOM data. Referenced in strategy review and competitive pricing discussions.

Issued immediately when a significant competitor product launch is detected: product description, key features, target market, pricing (where available), distribution channel, and competitive implications for the insurer. Distributed to product heads and distribution heads within 48 hours of detection.

Comprehensive annual strategic intelligence pack synthesising all year’s research: market size and penetration (EFInA, NIA, Swiss Re Sigma); macroeconomic environment (NBS, IMF); regulatory landscape update (NAICOM, NIIRA 2025 implementation); competitive landscape (market share, key competitor movements); technology and digital environment (GSMA, Insurtech monitoring); and strategic implications for the insurer’s three-year plan. Presented to Board and ExCo at the annual strategy review.

Issued when NAICOM or PenCom releases a new guideline, circular, or consultation document: summary of the key provisions, effective date, implications for the insurer’s operations, and recommended actions. Distributed to Compliance, Legal, Actuarial, and relevant business heads within 24 hours of publication.

blocks.h: Not every piece of intelligence is relevant to every stakeholder. Distributing every research output to every person on the ExCo creates information overload and reduces the probability that any specific finding is actually read and acted upon. The CI function should maintain a defined distribution matrix that matches each report type to the specific stakeholder groups for whom it is most relevant.

✓ = routine distribution; ◦ = selective distribution based on relevance; = not routinely distributed. The distribution matrix should be reviewed annually and updated when stakeholders’ roles or information needs change.

The most common failure mode of insurance research functions is not poor data or poor analysis; it is poor translation. Research that produces technically accurate findings but fails to make the ‘so what?’ explicit; research that arrives in a 50-page report when the decision-maker has 10 minutes; research that is produced by the strategy team after the relevant decision has already been made, these failures make the investment in research vanish without trace.

The research-to-strategy review is a monthly meeting (45–60 minutes) between the Head of Research/CI and the heads of strategy, product, distribution, and marketing, at which new research findings are shared, interpreted, and translated into specific management actions. The review disciplines the research function to produce decision-ready outputs on a regular cadence, rather than producing comprehensive reports that may or may not be read.
The review has a defined agenda:

items.h: Research updates: What new data or intelligence has been received since the last meeting? What are the key findings in three sentences or fewer?
Management implications: What, if anything, should we do differently as a result of these findings? Who owns the action?
Open research questions: What questions is the business trying to answer that the current research is not addressing? What new research should be commissioned?

blocks.h: The research function’s reports should be formatted for decision-making, not for filing. The ‘McKinsey one-pager’ principle applies: any finding that cannot be expressed as a clear headline, three to five supporting data points, and a recommended action in one to two pages is not yet decision-ready; it needs further synthesis. The full data and methodology should be available as an appendix, but the decision paper should stand alone without requiring the appendix to be read.

Every research output should answer four questions explicitly: What did we find? Why does it matter for our business? What should we do about it? Who owns the action and by when? If a research report cannot answer these four questions on its first page, the research has not been synthesised sufficiently for management use.

blocks.text: 36.10 Evaluating the Quality and Reliability of Research Sources

blocks.h: Not all research sources are equal in quality, reliability, or relevance. The research function must apply critical assessment criteria to every source, to avoid the trap of citing poor-quality data confidently because it happens to support a pre-existing conclusion.

rows: When was the data collected? Is it current enough to reflect the present state of the market?
Data more than 3–5 years old in a rapidly changing market; reports citing pre-pandemic data without adjustment.
Is the research method clearly described? Was the sample size appropriate? Was it nationally representative?
No methodology description; sample sizes below 500 for national claims; non-random or convenience sampling.
Is the research producer independent of the subject matter? Is there a potential conflict of interest in the findings?
Insurer-commissioned research claiming to show insurers perform well; trade association research showing the industry in a favourable light without independent verification.
Is the research specifically Nigerian, African, or from markets comparable enough for its findings to be applicable to the Nigerian context?
North American or European data cited as applicable to Nigeria without adjustment for market differences.
Has the research been peer-reviewed or editorially reviewed? Is it from an established institution with a track record of rigorous research?
Social media posts, unattributed blog content, or press releases cited as research evidence.
Are the data points internally consistent? Do totals add up? Are percentage claims mathematically verifiable?
Inconsistent figures across different sections of the same report; market size claims that significantly exceed published aggregates.

blocks.text: 36.11 Advisory: Building a Research-Driven Insurance Organisation

blocks.h: The research infrastructure described in this chapter is not the preserve of large insurance groups with dedicated teams and generous research budgets. A mid-size Nigerian life insurer with one skilled CI analyst, systematic access to freely available data sources (EFInA, NAICOM website, NIA publications, Swiss Re Sigma, Munich Re publications), and a disciplined monthly research review meeting can generate better strategic intelligence than a larger insurer with a larger team that produces beautiful reports that no one reads.

blocks.title: Advisory: Five Principles for Building Research-Driven Decision-Making

blocks.h: PRINCIPLE 1: MAKE DATA LITERACY A MANAGEMENT EXPECTATION. The CI function cannot succeed if its outputs are ignored by managers who do not value or trust quantitative evidence. The CEO and ExCo must model data-informed decision-making: explicitly asking for evidence when proposals are made; questioning strategy recommendations that are not grounded in market data; and recognising the CI function’s contribution to decisions that turn out well.

PRINCIPLE 2: START WITH THE FREELY AVAILABLE SOURCES. Before investing in premium subscriptions (Bloomberg, AXCO, specialist reports), the research function should systematically exploit the high-quality freely available data: EFInA surveys, NAICOM website, NIA publications, Swiss Re Sigma (free to download), Munich Re (free to download), IAIS publications (free), World Bank data (free), PenCom publications (free). An estimated 80% of the intelligence a Nigerian insurer needs for strategic planning is available for free; the 20% that requires subscription or commission should be prioritised where the intelligence gap is greatest.

PRINCIPLE 3: BUILD THE COMPETITOR DATABASE AS AN ONGOING EXERCISE, NOT AN ANNUAL TASK. A competitor that is monitored quarterly is understood; one that is reviewed annually provides a retrospective. The competitor financial profile for each top-five competitor should be updated at every NGX/CAC reporting cycle and every time NAICOM or the NIA publishes market data. This is a discipline, not a project.

PRINCIPLE 4: ENGAGE REGULATORS AS PARTNERS IN INTELLIGENCE, NOT JUST COMPLIANCE. A research function that treats NAICOM purely as a compliance authority misses one of the most valuable intelligence channels available. NAICOM staff know more about the Nigerian insurance market (its strengths, weaknesses, emerging risks, and trends) than any other institution. Building a constructive relationship with NAICOM’s supervision and policy teams, participating in industry consultations, and engaging thoughtfully on regulatory proposals generates intelligence and influence that no data subscription can replicate.

PRINCIPLE 5: MEASURE THE RESEARCH FUNCTION’S IMPACT ON DECISIONS, NOT ITS OUTPUT. A research function that produces 20 reports per year but influences three strategic decisions is less valuable than one that produces four focused intelligence briefs that change five management decisions. The CI function should track which of its outputs have influenced which decisions, and present this impact evidence to the ExCo annually as the justification for its budget.

blocks.title: The Highest-Value Single Research Investment for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: Commission a comprehensive primary research study, conducted every two years by an independent research agency, of 2,000+ current policyholders and 1,000+ non-insured individuals in the insurer’s target market segments. The study should explore: why policyholders chose the insurer’s product; what would cause them to lapse; what additional products they would buy; what unmet financial protection needs they have; and what the non-insured population would need to see from an insurance product to make it worth buying. This study, properly conducted and rigorously analysed, will generate more strategic insight than any amount of competitor monitoring or market data aggregation, because it answers the question that ultimately determines the insurer’s success: what do our customers and potential customers actually need, and are we giving it to them?
